coherence.reasons: Both build a clean pyramid to the same answer (Pro plan at +$12 per seat, usage allowance, mobile next). X groups its summary into why launch, which package, and trade-offs, and each slide title carries a quantified claim that traces to the appendix calculations. Its weakness is the 'only option' wording in the governing thought and slide 9, which its own table softens: the add-on also clears the margin floor and reaches the NRR target at the top of its range, and X admits the two overlap on ARR. Y's five-question structure is equally tidy, but its governing thought tells the reader to 'plan on about $2.9M' while its own slides say the 33% comes from another tier at another price and that half that rate misses the target. 'Beats the add-on on every test' and 'the revenue gain is near-certain' also sit uneasily with those caveats. X's headline range matches its body; Y's point estimate does not quite.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation and weigh the add-on, free-in-Core and mobile-first alternatives. X compares four options on seven criteria and plans on a range of $1.7–2.9M rather than the top of it. It adds a Q1 test on randomly chosen non-volunteer accounts with go/no-go thresholds, a Q3 review and an explicit fallback rule (reprice, never bundle free). It concedes that mobile-first 'may lose slightly less' on permanent ARR and names the breakpoints where the answer changes (26% and 21% migration, 75% mobile-fix effectiveness). Y also treats the mobile trade-off honestly ('narrowly', a 29% break-even, 'both meet the 2028 target') and conditions the case on engineers returning to mobile in Q3. But Y anchors the plan on the 33% precedent as a point estimate, has no pre-launch validation outside volunteers, and its only checkpoint is a six-month review. It also dismisses pure usage pricing and hiring quickly. X's argument that NRR timing decides the sequencing is somewhat stretched, but its staged, gated recommendation is the more defensible.

evidence.reasons: Both get the required calculations right: $8.06M vs $2.45M; inference of $32, $61 and $130 per account; 109 deals and $0.64M; Pro at $2.89M. Both rebut the Sales memo ($1.93M vs the $0.64M ceiling), flag Routewise's discount, and note the survey and beta biases. X goes further in three ways. It discounts the 14% paywall rate for volunteer bias (10.7% central, 7% low, flagged as an assumption). It catches two inconsistencies in the pack: the top decile's 58% share against the 40% implied by Table 2, and 1,190 churned accounts against the 1,372 implied. It also shows the regressive effect of a flat fee by account size and ties it to price being 22% of churn. Y has some sharp points of its own: renewal was measured while Copilot was free, the loss notes cover all lost deals rather than only Routewise ones, and usage is normalised per seat (444 per seat). But Y carries the unadjusted $2.5M and 33% figures into its headlines while calling them ceilings, and calls the Pro revenue gain 'near-certain' without support. X's 'only option' claim and its use of the 3.8-point mobile ceiling are mild overreaches.

revision.reasons: Both handle the CPO's hypothesis as the key expects: keep the launch, reject the $149 add-on and the $8M figure, and re-size from the paywall test with inference cost included. X does it explicitly and systematically. Slide 3 breaks the hypothesis into five conditions, marks which hold (value, need), which fail (46% take-up, flat-fee economics) and which hold conditionally (the mobile delay), and derives the revised answer from that. It then goes past the 14% to a 7–14% range because the paywall sample is also volunteers, and resets the plan number to a range. Y also revises properly (a 3.3x intent-to-purchase gap, and both signals treated as ceilings), but less explicitly as a test of the hypothesis. It then replaces one optimistic point estimate ($8M) with another un-discounted one ($2.9M from the 2023 precedent) as the planning figure.

overall.reasons: The two documents reach the same defensible recommendation with accurate core numbers, and both avoid all the traps in the key. X would serve the CEO better for four reasons: it plans on a range rather than the top-end precedent; it adds a pre-launch test on non-volunteers with explicit go/no-go and review thresholds; it spells out the decisions requested; and it surfaces the data inconsistencies and the sensitivities that would change the answer. Y is rigorous and in places more candid — it says both sequences meet the 2028 target and gives a 29% break-even for mobile-first. But its $2.9M headline, its 'near-certain' revenue claim and its thinner validation plan leave the decision maker more exposed if Pro migration falls short of the 2023 rate.
